title: He Wanted a Brotherhood. He Got a Funeral.
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Bradley argues that college men's longing for brotherhood is what opens the door to fraternity misconduct, and that the remedy is older men offering a better rite of passage. He first notes that state hazing laws, such as Vermont's, are so broad they have become a useless category that could cover scavenger hunts and youth group icebreakers. He then surveys recent reports from seven universities, including the death of 18-year-old Anthony Blas after a party with an unrecognized chapter at Cal State Fullerton, suspensions at UCLA, RIT, Baylor and Indiana, and a felony hazing plea at Northern Arizona. His analysis is that young men want a shared ordeal that proves their strength and binds them to one another, but lack models of how to do this in a way that builds character. Left alone, they invent their own rites, which become excessive or deadly. Drawing on his book Heroic Fraternity, he claims pledging can be shifted from vice to virtue quickly and ends by asking where the older men are.
points: Bradley contends that broad legal definitions of hazing blur the line between harmful abuse and ordinary group challenges.
Several of the reported chapters were already unrecognized by their schools, a point he flags for parents of pledges.
He reads hazing as a distorted attempt at a rite of passage rather than simple cruelty.
He claims none of the fraternities he has worked with in five years have had hazing infractions since shifting their intake process toward virtue.
His closing challenge is directed at older men, whom he sees as missing from the formation of young men.
quotes: As I travel the country and talk to college guys, it’s become apparent to me that college freshmen will allow themselves to be harmed for the sake of being included in a brotherhood.
The definition is so broad that something like sending pledges on a scavenger hunt could be considered hazing.

Young men want to belong. Some are willing to commit crimes or even put themselves at risk of death for it. Fraternities can give them friendships that help them grow up and take responsibility for others. But things can go wrong when it’s not guided by wisdom.

These stories persist mainly for one reason: guys want a rite of passage into adulthood and brotherhood, but young men lack models of what this looks like in a way that builds both camaraderie and character.

A rite of passage can accomplish this in a healthy way, but that won’t happen unless older men step in and provide better guidance. Otherwise, these young men are left to create their own rites of passage, which can become excessive or harmful.
Calling young men to virtue works, but they need older men to invite them into it. They also need help imagining the good they can do on their campuses by pursuing moral excellence.
